title: Reaching storage through a private endpoint

steps.n: Private DNS resolves the storage name to a private address inside the network.
The request travels over the private network to the endpoint, not to the internet.
The endpoint passes the request to the storage service.
The storage policy allows requests only from this private path and denies the public one.
The data returns over the same private path.
A request from outside the network is refused by the policy.
A principal tries to stop audit logging at night.
The control plane writes the event with who, what, where and when.
Logs flow to a separate account that few people can change.
A detection rule flags a change to logging as high risk.
The on-call engineer gets the alert with the principal and source address.
They restore logging, review recent actions and disable the identity if it is not legitimate.
A scanner reports a live key in a public repository.
The responder deactivates the key without deleting it, to keep evidence.
The audit log shows what the key did and from which addresses.
Attacker-created users, keys and servers are deleted.
The pipeline moves to a role with short-lived credentials.
Secret scanning and guardrails are added so the same path cannot recur.

title: A sign-in with conditional access
summary: Rules decide how strong the proof must be.

steps.n: The user opens the application and is sent to the sign-in service.
The policy looks at the user, device, location and risk of this attempt.
An unfamiliar location triggers a second factor requirement.
The user approves on their device.
A short-lived token is issued with the claims the application needs.
The application trusts the token and applies its own authorization.

title: A request through the API server

steps.n: kubectl sends a create request over TLS with a credential.
The API server identifies the caller from a certificate, token or sign-in.
RBAC checks whether this subject may create this kind in this namespace.
Controllers may change the object or reject it, for example by policy.
The validated object is written to etcd, the only place state is stored.
The caller receives the stored object, and controllers begin to act on it.

title: etcd and quorum
summary: Why a majority of members is needed.

steps.n: The API server sends a write to the etcd leader.
The leader sends the entry to the followers.
The same entry goes to the other follower.
One follower confirms, which together with the leader is a majority of three.
With a majority the leader commits and tells the API server the write succeeded.
The cluster keeps working with two of three, but losing a second member stops writes.
Nothing should write while state is being replaced.
The status command confirms the file is readable and shows its key count.
Every member gets a new data directory built from the same snapshot.
The members form a new cluster with the new membership settings.
The API servers connect and serve the restored state.
Objects created after the snapshot are re-applied from the repository, and the team checks volumes separately.

title: Upgrading a cluster one minor version

steps.n: Read release notes, scan for removed APIs and take an etcd snapshot.
The first control plane node is upgraded, then the others.
A worker node is made unschedulable and its pods are evicted.
The kubelet and packages are updated and restarted.
The node is schedulable again and pods return.
Smoke tests and dashboards confirm the services are healthy before the next node.

title: A node drain step by step

steps.n: The node is marked unschedulable so nothing new lands on it.
The drain asks the eviction API to remove each pod.
An eviction is refused if it would break the disruption budget.
When allowed, the pod is terminated gracefully.
The owning controller makes a new pod and the scheduler places it on another node.
After the work the node is opened for scheduling again.
A service account asks to list secrets in the shop namespace.
The API server finds role bindings that mention this subject in that namespace.
The bound role lists the verbs and resources it allows.
The role allows pods but not secrets, so nothing allows the request.
The caller receives an error naming the subject, verb and resource.
A new rule allows only list on secrets in that namespace.
The team raises replicas from 10 to 14.
The controller asks the API server to create four more pods.
Admission adds the new requests to the namespace usage and compares with the hard limit.
The creation fails with an exceeded quota message.
The team reads the event on the ReplicaSet.
They reduce oversized requests or ask for a higher quota through review.
Load rises and the HPA increases the replica count.
No node has enough free requests for the new pods.
The autoscaler sees unschedulable pods and calculates a node size that fits them.
It asks the cloud to add a node to the pool.
The node registers and the scheduler places the pending pods.
Under-used nodes are drained and removed when pods can move safely.
A packet leaves the web pod for the API pod.
The plugin checks that egress from the web pod to the API on this port is allowed.
It checks the API pod's ingress allows traffic from web pods.
Both lists allow it, so the request is delivered and answered.
A direct call from the web pod to the database is attempted.
No policy allows it, so the packet is dropped and nothing reaches the database.
A manifest asks for privileged mode and host networking.
Pod Security admission reads the namespace's profile label.
The pod spec is checked against the baseline rules.
Privileged mode violates the baseline, so the request is refused with a clear message.
The developer removes the extra powers and sets a non-root security context.
The hardened pod passes admission and starts.
The kubelet sends regular heartbeats that update the node lease.
The disk fills and the kubelet stops reporting.
The node controller sees no update within the grace period.
The node condition is set and taints are added.
After the toleration period, pods on the node are marked for removal.
Controllers create replacements and the scheduler places them on healthy nodes.
Cluster certificates are created with a one year lifetime.
A monitor tracks the days left on each certificate.
At 30 days an alert reaches the operator.
The operator renews the certificates with the cluster tools.
The control plane components are restarted to load the new files.
An unnoticed expiry breaks every client connection to the API server.
CI builds the image and publishes it to the registry.
CI changes the image tag in the configuration repository and stops there.
The controller in the cluster detects the new commit.
It renders the manifests and compares them with live state.
The controller applies the difference from inside the cluster.
The result shows as Synced and Healthy; CI never held cluster credentials.
The repo server clones the repository at the target revision.
Helm, Kustomize or plain YAML is turned into manifests.
The controller reads the matching objects from the cluster.
Differences between desired and live state are calculated.
With automation on, the controller applies the difference.
The loop runs again on new commits or when live state changes.

title: Creating the first Application
summary: From install to a running service.

steps.n: The components start in their own namespace.
A read-only credential is added for the configuration repository.
The manifest names the source path and the destination namespace.
Argo CD reads the folder and renders the manifests.
Nothing is deployed yet, so the application is OutOfSync.
The engineer presses sync and the objects appear and become Healthy.
An engineer changes the replica count directly in the cluster.
The controller sees live state no longer matches the repository.
The application is shown as OutOfSync with a diff.
With self-heal on, the controller applies the repository value again.
The replica count returns to the committed number.
The engineer makes the change in the repository so it lasts.
Argo CD applies the rendered manifests.
Live state matches desired state, so the sync status is Synced.
The image tag is wrong and pods go into CrashLoopBackOff.
Argo CD evaluates the Deployment and finds it not available.
The dashboard shows Synced and Degraded together.
The team looks at events and logs, not at the manifest diff.
A manifest for an old service is removed from the repository.
The controller sees an object in the cluster that is no longer in the source.
The object has no Prune=false annotation, so it may be deleted.
With prune on, the controller deletes the object.
Databases and volumes carry the annotation so they survive a mistake.
A render check in the pull request shows what would be removed.
The Application names an exact chart version.
The environment's values file in the repository is selected.
The repo server runs the equivalent of helm template with those values.
The rendered manifests are applied as plain objects.
Helm itself keeps no release, because Argo CD tracks the resources.
A change to a value shows up as a reviewed difference.
One Application points at a folder of Application manifests.
Syncing creates each child Application.
Each child delivers its own service to the cluster.
A new Application manifest is committed to the folder.
The parent creates the new Application automatically.
The new service is delivered with no extra clicks.
A generator lists staging and production, or every registered cluster.
The template inserts each target's name and path.
One Application is created per target.
Each application syncs to its own cluster and namespace.
A new cluster is registered and the generator sees it.
A new Application is created and delivers the same service.
The new image tag is committed to the staging overlay.
Staging delivers the version and tests run.
The same tag is proposed for the production overlay in a pull request.
A reviewer checks the diff, test results and timing.
The merge is the approval and leaves an audit record.
Production delivers the same version that was tested in staging.

title: Waves and hooks in a sync

steps.n: The controller sorts resources by sync wave.
Namespaces and CRDs are applied first and must become healthy.
A migration Job runs before the application changes.
The controller waits for the Job to finish successfully.
The Deployment and Service are applied.
A smoke test runs and the hook is cleaned up when it succeeds.

title: A canary rollout with analysis
summary: Gradual traffic with a safety net.

steps.n: A small number of pods run the new version.
A traffic rule sends five percent of requests to the canary.
Analysis queries the error rate for the canary.
The error rate is under the threshold, so the rollout advances to 25 percent.
If the threshold is crossed, traffic returns to the stable pods automatically.
After the last step the canary becomes the stable version.
Team A defines an application that targets team B's namespace.
The project's allowed destinations list only team A namespaces.
Sync is refused with a message that the destination is not permitted.
Team A points the application at its own namespace.
The destination is allowed, so the sync proceeds.
The project also blocks cluster-level kinds that the team has no need for.

title: Secrets without storing them in the repository
summary: A reference instead of a value.

steps.n: The repository holds a resource that names a secret, not its value.
Argo CD applies the reference object to the cluster.
The operator reads the real value from the cloud secrets manager with its own identity.
A Secret is created in the namespace for the pods to use.
Argo CD ignores the generated Secret contents so they never appear in diffs.
A new value in the manager is picked up automatically on the next refresh.
A command adds the remote cluster and creates a service account there.
The token is saved in the hub as a secret, so the hub namespace must be protected.
The application's destination uses the remote cluster's address.
The hub applies the rendered manifests to the remote cluster.
The remote resources' health is reported back to the hub.
The service account in the target has only the rights the applications need.
argocd app get shows which stage failed first.
A bad credential or path fails here with a clear message.
The same helm template or kustomize build is run locally to reproduce errors.
A forbidden or not permitted message points to RBAC or project rules.
If everything applied, the pods are debugged with events and logs.
The fix and a prevention are written down.

title: How a signal reaches a process

steps.n: The kill command asks the kernel to deliver SIGTERM to the process ID.
The kernel records the signal for the target process.
If the program installed a handler, it runs and begins an orderly shutdown.
The handler finishes requests, flushes buffers and releases locks.
If the process ignores SIGTERM, a later SIGKILL is sent.
SIGKILL cannot be caught, so the kernel removes the process at once.

title: How a file write reaches the disk

steps.n: The program writes bytes, which go to memory in the page cache.
The call returns before the data is on disk.
The cache marks pages dirty and the kernel flushes them in the background.
A program that needs durability asks for the data to be flushed.
The filesystem writes data and its journal to the disk.
Only after the disk reports completion does fsync return, so a crash no longer loses the data.
The feature branch has twelve small commits, including fixes.
Reviewers approve the combined change.
Git combines the twelve commits into one new commit on main.
The history shows one commit with a clear message and a link to the review.
The old branch still has the twelve commits and is deleted.
If it causes trouble, one revert undoes the whole feature.
A hard reset moves the branch back and the last three commits vanish from view.
Git recorded every previous position of the branch tip.
The developer runs git reflog and finds the commit before the reset.
A new branch is created at that commit.
All three commits are reachable again.
The developer merges or cherry-picks the work back where it belongs.

title: Reading a file line by line safely

steps.n: The script redirects the file into a while loop.
The read command takes a line, with IFS= and -r so spaces and backslashes survive.
The loop passes the line to a command inside quotes.
A command that reads standard input would swallow the rest of the file.
The loop continues until read returns end of file.
The script checks the status and stops on failure.

title: A script that refuses to run twice

steps.n: Cron starts the script on schedule.
The script uses flock to take an exclusive lock on a lock file.
The long task runs while holding the lock.
A late job starts while the first is still running.
The second run cannot get the lock and exits quietly.
When the first run ends, the lock is released automatically.
The developer updates the version in the project metadata.
The build tool creates a source archive and a wheel.
The files are uploaded to a package index with a scoped token.
The index stores the files and lists the new version.
A user installs the package, preferably with a pinned version.
Hashes and a lock file ensure the same files are used each time.

title: A Python tool exits with the right code

steps.n: The script calls an API and the call fails.
The handler catches the specific exception and logs a clear message.
It exits with a non-zero code instead of returning normally.
The shell stores the exit status for the caller.
The pipeline step fails and the team is notified.
On success the script exits with zero and later steps continue.
